name: Big Ben
blurb: Strictly the name of the bell, not the tower — which is the Elizabeth Tower.

name: Eiffel Tower
blurb: Meant to stand for 20 years; radio antennas saved it from the scrap heap.

name: Colosseum
blurb: In its early years the arena could be flooded for mock naval battles.

name: Taj Mahal
blurb: A tomb, not a palace: Shah Jahan built it for a wife who died bearing their 14th child.

name: Machu Picchu
blurb: The Spanish never found it — which is a big part of why it is still here.

name: Petra
blurb: Carved by the Nabataeans, whose real genius was plumbing water through the desert.

name: Angkor Wat
blurb: The largest religious monument on Earth, and it appears on Cambodia's flag.

name: Christ the Redeemer
blurb: Clad in soapstone tiles glued on by volunteers, some of whom wrote wishes on the backs.

name: Great Pyramid of Giza
blurb: The only ancient wonder still standing — and the world's tallest building for 3,800 years.

name: Sagrada Família
blurb: Under construction since 1882; Gaudí shrugged that his client was not in a hurry.

name: Hagia Sophia
blurb: Cathedral for 900 years, mosque for 500, museum for 85 — and now a mosque again.

name: Golden Gate Bridge
blurb: Its famous color, International Orange, started life as mere primer paint.

name: Sydney Opera House
blurb: Its Danish architect quit mid-build and never returned to see it finished.

name: Chichén Itzá
blurb: At the equinox, the pyramid's shadow becomes a serpent slithering down the staircase.

name: Stonehenge
blurb: The bluestones were hauled some 250 km from Wales — nobody is quite sure how.

name: Borobudur
blurb: Nine stacked platforms lay buried under volcanic ash for centuries before rediscovery.

name: Alhambra
blurb: Its walls repeat the motto 'There is no victor but God' thousands of times.

name: Neuschwanstein Castle
blurb: Ludwig II's fantasy castle bankrupted him; Disney later borrowed the look.

name: Moai of Rapa Nui
blurb: Nearly 900 statues, and almost all of them face inland, watching the islanders.

name: Terracotta Army
blurb: Farmers digging a well in 1974 found 8,000 soldiers — every face different.

name: Statue of Liberty
blurb: Her copper skin is thinner than two pennies; the green is a century of patina.

name: Great Wall of China
blurb: Not visible from space with the naked eye, whatever the myth insists.

name: Leaning Tower of Pisa
blurb: It began leaning before the third floor was even built — the soil never stood a chance.

name: Mount Rushmore
blurb: Jefferson began on Washington's right, cracked, and was blasted off and re-carved on the left.

name: Parthenon
blurb: Its columns bulge and lean inward on purpose — optical tricks to look perfectly straight.

name: Saint Basil's Cathedral
blurb: Legend claims Ivan the Terrible blinded the architect so he could never build a rival.

name: Burj Khalifa
blurb: So tall you can watch sunset at the base, ride the lift up, and watch it set again.

name: Itsukushima Floating Torii
blurb: At high tide the great gate floats; at low tide you can walk out and touch it.

name: Forbidden City
blurb: 980 buildings, and for 500 years entering without permission meant death.

name: Potala Palace
blurb: A 13-story palace at 3,700 m — the Dalai Lama's winter home until 1959.

name: Mont-Saint-Michel
blurb: The tide races in here so fast that Victor Hugo compared it to galloping horses.

name: Brandenburg Gate
blurb: Napoleon stole the chariot on top and took it to Paris; it came home after Waterloo.

name: Palace of Versailles
blurb: Started as a hunting lodge; ended with 2,300 rooms and a hall made of mirrors.

name: Abu Simbel
blurb: The whole temple was sawn into blocks and moved uphill in the 1960s to dodge a reservoir.

name: Valley of the Kings
blurb: Sixty-plus royal tombs, and only Tutankhamun's was found nearly intact.

name: Petronas Towers
blurb: Built by rival contractors, one tower each, racing floor by floor to the top.

name: Marina Bay Sands
blurb: Three towers balancing a ship on top, with the world's longest rooftop infinity pool.

name: Golden Temple of Amritsar
blurb: Its kitchen serves free meals to up to 100,000 visitors a day, every single day.

name: Grand Palace, Bangkok
blurb: Home of the Emerald Buddha — which is actually carved from green jade, not emerald.

name: Shwedagon Pagoda
blurb: Plated in real gold and topped with thousands of gems, including a 76-carat diamond.

name: Charles Bridge
blurb: Charles IV laid the first stone at 5:31 on 9.7.1357 — a palindrome picked by astrologers.

name: Hollywood Sign
blurb: It originally read HOLLYWOODLAND — an advertisement for a housing development.

name: CN Tower
blurb: World's tallest free-standing structure for 32 years; you can walk its rim on a harness.

name: Panama Canal
blurb: Ships climb 26 m over the continental divide in water-filled steps.

name: Teotihuacan
blurb: Its builders' name is lost; Teotihuacan is what the Aztecs called the ruins centuries later.

name: Windmills of Kinderdijk
blurb: Nineteen windmills from the 1730s, built to pump a country that sits below the sea.

name: The Little Mermaid
blurb: Repeatedly decapitated by vandals and once blown off her rock — she keeps coming back.

name: Dome of the Rock
blurb: One of the oldest Islamic buildings on Earth, its dome finished in 691 CE.

name: Space Needle
blurb: Built for the 1962 World's Fair in about 400 days, on a plot bought for $75,000.

name: Hoover Dam
blurb: Poured in blocks because a single mass of concrete would take a century to cool.

name: Kaaba, Mecca
blurb: Over a billion people face this cube five times a day, wherever they are on Earth.

name: Hassan II Mosque
blurb: Part of its floor is glass over the Atlantic, and its minaret fires a laser toward Mecca.

name: Edinburgh Castle
blurb: Built on an extinct volcano that last erupted 340 million years ago.

name: Sensō-ji Temple
blurb: Tokyo's oldest temple, founded in 645 after two fishermen netted a golden statue.

name: Red Fort
blurb: The Mughal emperors' sandstone fort — India's PM raises the flag here each Independence Day.

name: Sahara Desert
blurb: Roughly the size of the United States, and it was green savanna just 6,000 years ago.

name: Amazon Rainforest
blurb: Makes rivers in the sky — its trees pump out around 20 billion tonnes of vapor a day.

name: Mount Everest
blurb: Grows about 4 mm a year, and its summit rock is marine limestone from an ancient seafloor.

name: Great Barrier Reef
blurb: The largest living structure on Earth — visible from orbit.

name: Grand Canyon
blurb: The rocks at the bottom are nearly half as old as the planet itself.

name: Lake Baikal
blurb: Holds one fifth of Earth's unfrozen fresh water — more than all the Great Lakes combined.

name: Mount Kilimanjaro
blurb: Three volcanoes in one, wearing glaciers three degrees south of the equator — for now.

name: Victoria Falls
blurb: Locals call it Mosi-oa-Tunya: the smoke that thunders.

name: Dead Sea
blurb: The lowest land on Earth, and its shoreline drops about a metre further every year.

name: Iguazu Falls
blurb: Nearly 300 separate falls; on seeing them Eleanor Roosevelt reportedly sighed 'poor Niagara'.

name: Ural Mountains
blurb: The classic dividing line between Europe and Asia, and one of Earth's oldest ranges.

name: Gobi Desert
blurb: A cold desert — winters can hit minus 40 while the dunes wear snow.

name: Danube River
blurb: Flows through ten countries, more than any other river on Earth.

name: Nile Delta
blurb: Herodotus coined the word 'delta' here — the river fans out like the Greek letter.

name: Uluru
blurb: Most of it is underground, like an iceberg of sandstone.

name: Mount Fuji
blurb: A near-perfect cone that last erupted in 1707; climbing season is two months a year.

name: Niagara Falls
blurb: In 1969 engineers switched off the American Falls entirely to study the rock face.

name: Serengeti
blurb: Over a million wildebeest loop through here yearly in the largest land migration on Earth.

name: Okavango Delta
blurb: A river that never reaches the sea — it fans out and vanishes into the Kalahari sands.

name: Mount Vesuvius
blurb: The only volcano to erupt on mainland Europe in the last century — 3 million people nearby.

name: Loch Ness
blurb: Holds more water than every lake in England and Wales combined — monster not included.

name: Kalahari Desert
blurb: Not a true desert — it rains too much — but the sand swallows the water instantly.

name: Andes
blurb: The longest mountain range on land, running 7,000 km down an entire continent.

name: Rocky Mountains
blurb: The spine of North America — rain falling here parts for the Pacific or the Atlantic.

name: Matterhorn
blurb: Its summit rock is a chunk of Africa, shoved onto Europe when the continents collided.

name: Mississippi River
blurb: Drains 40 percent of the continental US; the name is Ojibwe for 'great river'.

name: Ganges River
blurb: Sacred to a billion people; its headwaters pour from an ice cave called the Cow's Mouth.

name: Nile River
blurb: Long crowned the world's longest river — though the Amazon keeps disputing the title.

name: Patagonia
blurb: Named for a mythical race of giants the first European visitors swore lived here.

name: Great Rift Valley
blurb: The continent is slowly unzipping here; give it a few million years and East Africa sails off.

name: Mount Etna
blurb: Europe's most active volcano — the ancient Greeks parked the monster Typhon beneath it.

name: Bora Bora
blurb: A sinking volcano wearing a coral ring — eventually only the lagoon will remain.

name: Yellowstone
blurb: The world's first national park sits inside the caldera of a supervolcano.

name: Kīlauea
blurb: One of Earth's most active volcanoes; it erupted almost non-stop from 1983 to 2018.

name: Galápagos Islands
blurb: The finches here nudged Darwin toward evolution — though he nearly overlooked them.

name: Lake Victoria
blurb: Africa's largest lake, and the long-debated source of the Nile.

name: Table Mountain
blurb: Its flat top hosts more plant species than the entire United Kingdom.

name: Göbekli Tepe
blurb: Temples 6,000 years older than Stonehenge — raised before farming, then deliberately buried.

name: Timbuktu
blurb: Once traded gold for salt at equal weight, and held hundreds of thousands of manuscripts.

name: Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela
blurb: Eleven churches carved downward into solid rock — you look down at the rooftops.

name: Nazca Lines
blurb: Figures so large they were only recognized from the air; the hummingbird spans 90 metres.

name: Great Zimbabwe
blurb: Medieval walls 11 m high with no mortar at all — the country renamed itself after these ruins.

name: Registan, Samarkand
blurb: Three madrasas facing one square — the Silk Road's grandest classroom.

name: Temples of Bagan
blurb: Over 2,000 temples scattered across one river plain — down from perhaps 10,000.

name: Meteora Monasteries
blurb: Monasteries perched on rock pillars; supplies once arrived by rope and net — monks included.

name: Pamukkale
blurb: The 'cotton castle': hot springs have glazed an entire hillside in white travertine.

name: Wadi Rum
blurb: Lawrence of Arabia's desert, now Hollywood's go-to stand-in for Mars.

name: Mesa Verde Cliff Dwellings
blurb: Whole villages built into cliff alcoves, then abandoned in the 1200s — nobody is sure why.

name: Carthage
blurb: Rome razed it, allegedly salted it, then rebuilt it as one of its own greatest cities.

name: Persepolis
blurb: Alexander burned it; historians still argue whether it was policy or a party gone wrong.

name: Leptis Magna
blurb: One of Rome's best-preserved cities, kept intact by centuries under Saharan sand.

name: Mohenjo-daro
blurb: A 4,500-year-old city with street grids and sewers — and a script nobody has cracked.

name: Sigiriya
blurb: A palace atop a 200 m rock column, ringed by mirror walls and 1,500-year-old graffiti.

name: Tikal
blurb: A Maya superpower swallowed by jungle; its temples cameo as a rebel base in Star Wars.

name: Tiwanaku
blurb: Its stones were cut so precisely that colonial Spaniards blamed giants.

name: Hampi
blurb: Capital of Vijayanagara, once among the world's richest cities; its ruins sprawl for miles.

name: Cappadocia
blurb: Volcanic ash carved into fairy chimneys, with cities dug ten storeys underground.

name: Skellig Michael
blurb: Monks lived on this sea crag for 600 years; Luke Skywalker retired here much later.

name: Three Gorges Dam
blurb: Its reservoir shifted enough water to measurably slow Earth's rotation — by microseconds.

name: Chernobyl
blurb: The exclusion zone has become an accidental wildlife refuge, wolves and all.

name: Salar de Uyuni
blurb: After rain, the world's largest salt flat becomes a mirror the size of Jamaica.

name: Socotra
blurb: A third of its plants exist nowhere else, including umbrella trees that bleed red resin.

name: Kamchatka Peninsula
blurb: Three hundred volcanoes, 29 of them active — and until 1990 no outsiders were allowed in.

name: Ha Long Bay
blurb: Legend says a descending dragon spat these 1,600 limestone islands into the sea.

name: Mount Roraima
blurb: A tabletop mountain so isolated it inspired Conan Doyle's The Lost World.

name: Danakil Depression
blurb: Neon acid springs, salt plains and 50-degree heat — one of the hottest places on Earth.

name: Lake Turkana
blurb: The Jade Sea — a desert lake whose shores keep yielding our oldest ancestors.

name: Zhangjiajie
blurb: Thousands of quartzite pillars — the inspiration for Avatar's floating mountains.

name: Sossusvlei
blurb: Dunes over 300 m tall surround a clay pan of 900-year-old dead trees.

name: Plitvice Lakes
blurb: Sixteen terraced lakes that keep building their own travertine dams.

name: Giant's Causeway
blurb: About 40,000 hexagonal basalt columns; myth credits a giant building a road to Scotland.

name: Cliffs of Moher
blurb: Sea cliffs rising 214 m sheer from the Atlantic, home to 30,000 nesting seabirds.

name: Angel Falls
blurb: The world's tallest waterfall — much of the water turns to mist before landing 979 m below.

name: Pantanal
blurb: The world's largest tropical wetland — better jaguar-spotting than the Amazon.

name: Atacama Desert
blurb: Some weather stations here have never recorded rain; NASA tests Mars rovers on its soil.

name: Aconcagua
blurb: The tallest mountain outside Asia — nearly 7 km up, yet climbable without ropes.

name: Denali
blurb: Measured from its own base to peak, it out-rises Everest.

name: Lake Titicaca
blurb: The highest navigable lake on Earth, still plied by boats woven from reeds.

name: Purnululu (Bungle Bungles)
blurb: Beehive-striped domes outsiders only 'found' in 1983 — locals had known for 20,000 years.

name: Milford Sound
blurb: Up to 7 m of rain a year feeds waterfalls that pour straight into the fjord.

name: Band-e Amir Lakes
blurb: Six impossibly blue lakes held up by natural travertine dams, high in the Hindu Kush.

name: Tsingy de Bemaraha
blurb: A forest of limestone needles so sharp they can slice through boots.

name: Mount Ararat
blurb: The dormant giant of Armenian identity — which stands just across the border, in Turkey.

name: K2
blurb: Deadlier than Everest, and never climbed in winter until 2021.

name: Bhutan
blurb: The dragon grips jewels in its claws; Bhutan calls itself Druk Yul — Land of the Thunder Dragon.

name: Kiribati
blurb: A frigatebird over a Pacific sunrise — flown by the only country in all four hemispheres.

name: Turkmenistan
blurb: The stripe shows five real carpet patterns, one for each major Turkmen tribe.

name: Eswatini
blurb: The shield and spears are real Emasotsha regiment gear; the country renamed itself in 2018.

name: Kyrgyzstan
blurb: That sun holds a yurt — the crossed roof-crown you would see lying inside one, looking up.

name: Mozambique
blurb: The only national flag bearing a modern rifle — an AK-47 crossed with a hoe.

name: Papua New Guinea
blurb: A bird-of-paradise on red and black, designed by a 15-year-old schoolgirl in 1971.

name: Saint Lucia
blurb: The triangles are the Pitons, twin volcanic spires rising straight out of the Caribbean.

name: Vanuatu
blurb: The yellow Y traces the archipelago's shape; the boar's tusk stands for prosperity.

name: Belize
blurb: One of only two national flags with humans on it — two woodcutters and a mahogany tree.

name: Dominica
blurb: Stars a sisserou parrot — one of the very few purple things on any national flag.

name: Seychelles
blurb: Five rays fanning out like a sunrise, for a nation scattered across 115 islands.

name: Fiji
blurb: Still carries the Union Jack, plus a shield where a lion holds a cocoa pod.

name: Albania
blurb: The double-headed eagle of Skanderbeg, watching east and west since the 1400s.

name: Uganda
blurb: Six bold stripes and a grey crowned crane — a design settled on in a matter of weeks in 1962.

name: Kazakhstan
blurb: A steppe eagle soars under a 32-ray sun, beside a golden ornament stripe.

name: Barbados
blurb: The trident is deliberately broken — Neptune's shaft snapped to mark the break with Britain.

name: Grenada
blurb: A nutmeg pod sits on the hoist — this one island grows a fifth of the world's supply.

name: Cyprus
blurb: One of the few flags showing its own map — in copper, the metal named after the island.

name: Chile
blurb: Some 4,300 km long and on average just 180 km wide — a ribbon pinned between Andes and ocean.

name: Italy
blurb: The boot — permanently mid-kick, with Sicily as the ball.

name: The Gambia
blurb: A river with borders: essentially the Gambia River plus about 25 km on either bank.

name: Norway
blurb: Count the fjords and islands and its coastline unravels to over 100,000 km.

name: Vietnam
blurb: Locals see a bamboo pole balancing two rice baskets — the deltas at either end.

name: Madagascar
blurb: The world's fourth-largest island, adrift from Africa long enough to invent lemurs.

name: Namibia
blurb: That odd panhandle — the Caprivi Strip — exists because Germany wanted a route to the Zambezi.

name: Malawi
blurb: A sliver of a country wrapped around the third-largest lake in Africa.

name: Cuba
blurb: Cubans call their island 'el cocodrilo' — from above, it really does lounge like one.

name: Croatia
blurb: Its croissant shape wraps around Bosnia, leaving the neighbour just 20 km of coast.

name: Somalia
blurb: The number 7 of the Horn of Africa, with the mainland continent's longest coastline.

name: Panama
blurb: The isthmus twists so much that here you can watch the sun rise over the Pacific.

name: Mongolia
blurb: Sandwiched between two giants, and the most sparsely populated country on Earth.

name: Laos
blurb: The only landlocked country in Southeast Asia, hugging the Mekong for some 1,800 km.

name: Portugal
blurb: Holder of some of Europe's oldest fixed borders — essentially unchanged since 1297.

name: Point Nemo
blurb: The farthest point from land on Earth — the nearest humans are often astronauts overhead.

name: Tristan da Cunha
blurb: The most remote inhabited island on Earth: about 240 people, one settlement, no airport.

name: Bouvet Island
blurb: The most remote island of all — an uninhabited glacier cap that Norway somehow owns.

name: Nauru
blurb: The smallest island nation — once, briefly, the world's richest country per head, on bird guano.

name: Kiritimati
blurb: The largest coral atoll on Earth, and among the first inhabited places to greet each new year.

name: Svalbard
blurb: Polar bears outnumber people, and the Global Seed Vault keeps crop backups in the permafrost.

name: Jan Mayen
blurb: A volcanic Norwegian outpost with 18 rotating station staff and zero permanent residents.

name: Diego Garcia
blurb: A secretive military atoll; its displaced Chagossian islanders are still fighting to return.

name: Kerguelen Islands
blurb: The Desolation Islands — French, treeless, and reachable only by ship a few times a year.

name: Wrangel Island
blurb: Woolly mammoths survived here until about 1650 BCE — after the pyramids were built.

name: Pitcairn Island
blurb: Settled by the Bounty mutineers in 1790; around 40 of their descendants remain.

name: Tuvalu
blurb: Highest point about 4.6 m — it earns real money licensing its .tv internet domain.

name: Comoros
blurb: The Perfume Isles, world capital of ylang-ylang — and of coups, with 20-odd attempts since 1975.

name: São Tomé and Príncipe
blurb: Chocolate islands on the equator — by 1908 Portuguese planters made it the top cocoa producer.

name: Niue
blurb: One of the smallest countries on Earth — a raised coral island of about 1,700 people.

name: Andorra la Vella
blurb: Europe's highest capital, in a country whose co-head of state is the President of France.

name: Vaduz
blurb: A capital of 5,700 people below the prince's castle — Liechtenstein has no airport at all.

name: Ngerulmud
blurb: The world's least populous capital — Palau's purpose-built government complex on a hill.

name: Yamoussoukro
blurb: Côte d'Ivoire's official capital, with a basilica larger than St. Peter's in Rome.

name: Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte
blurb: Sri Lanka's actual capital — Colombo gets the fame, Kotte keeps the parliament.

name: Nuuk
blurb: One of the world's smallest capitals, governing the world's largest island.

name: Oymyakon
blurb: The coldest inhabited place on Earth — once minus 67.7 C, and school stays open past minus 50.

name: La Rinconada
blurb: The highest permanent settlement on Earth — a gold-mining town at 5,100 m with no plumbing.

name: Coober Pedy
blurb: Opal capital of the world, where summer heat drives half the town to live underground.

name: Alert, Nunavut
blurb: The northernmost permanently inhabited place on Earth, 817 km from the Pole.

name: Darién Gap
blurb: The only break in the Pan-American Highway — 100 km of roadless swamp and jungle.

name: Kuril Islands
blurb: Russia and Japan never signed a WWII peace treaty, largely because of these islands.

name: Lake Vostok
blurb: A lake the size of Lake Ontario sealed under 4 km of ice for perhaps 15 million years.

name: Challenger Deep
blurb: Nearly 11 km down — Everest would sink here with over 2 km of water to spare.

name: Zealandia
blurb: A drowned eighth continent, 94 percent underwater — New Zealand is just its high ground.

name: Aral Sea
blurb: Once the world's fourth-largest lake, drained for cotton until ships stood in open desert.

name: Sargasso Sea
blurb: A sea with no coastline, bounded only by currents — where the world's eels go to spawn.

name: Bermuda Triangle
blurb: Statistically no more dangerous than any other patch of busy ocean — but a better story.

name: McMurdo Station
blurb: Antarctica's largest settlement — about 1,000 summer residents, ATMs and a coffee house.

name: South Pole
blurb: The station sits on drifting ice, so the pole marker has to be re-planted every year.

name: Saint-Pierre and Miquelon
blurb: A leftover piece of France 25 km off Canada — baguettes, euros and all.

name: Norfolk Island
blurb: Resettled by Pitcairn's Bounty descendants in 1856; many still speak Norf'k.

name: Rub' al Khali
blurb: The Empty Quarter — Earth's largest sand sea, with dunes the size of small mountains.

name: Lake Natron
blurb: Its caustic red water can calcify birds — yet flamingos breed here because nothing else can.

name: Darvaza Gas Crater
blurb: The Door to Hell — a gas crater set alight in 1971 that has burned ever since.

name: Mount Thor
blurb: Earth's greatest sheer cliff — 1,250 m of granite that actually overhangs.

name: Richat Structure
blurb: The Eye of the Sahara — a 40 km bullseye that astronauts use as a landmark from orbit.

name: Lençóis Maranhenses
blurb: A desert of white dunes that fills with thousands of turquoise rain lagoons every year.

name: Chatham Islands
blurb: In their own time zone, 45 minutes ahead of New Zealand — among the first to see sunrise.

name: Macquarie Island
blurb: Every royal penguin on Earth breeds on this one subantarctic island.

name: Taklamakan Desert
blurb: Its name is popularly glossed as 'you go in, you don't come out'; the Silk Road split to avoid it.

name: Mount Paektu
blurb: The sacred volcano of both Koreas — North Korean legend places Kim Jong Il's birth here.
